\newcommand{\Ju}{\mathrm{Ju}}
\newcommand{\Ad}{\mathrm{Ad}}
\newcommand{\Tot}{\mathrm{Tot}}

# Introduction

A graph is a set of vertices (also called nodes) and edges that connect
(some of) the vertices.  They have applications in a number of fields.
Acyclic directed graphs (abbreviated DAGs) are one special type of graph
in which the edges are directed---they are drawn as arrows that start at one 
vertex and end at another.  If an arrow extends from node $A$ to node $C$ and
from node $B$ to node $C$, then $A$ and $B$ are referred to as _parents_ of
$C$, and $C$ is called a _daughter_ of nodes $A$ and $B$.  (Note that
these terms are completely separate from the parent-offspring relatinships we
deal with in CKMR!).  

In statistics, DAGs are particularly useful because if a joint probability
distribution can be factorized into a product of conditional probabilities,
then that factorization can be reprsented as a DAG.  Quite simply, if each
variable involved in the joint probability is associated with a vertex, 
then the factorization of the joint probability can be described as a product
over vertices of the conditional probability of each vertex given its parents.
Representing a joint distribution in that manner provides access to a variety
of graphical interpretations and algorithms which can serve to make calculations
such as conditioning on observed values or marginalization efficient.
(For a somewhat baroque example of this in the inference of pedigrees from
genetic data, see @anderson2016bayesian).  The DAG representation also
provides a compact visual overview of the variables in the joint probability
distribuion (i.e., the "model") and their relationships with one another. Such
a visual representation can be useful for understanding and comparing the
structure of different models.  

I have found DAGs (and other graphical flavors) to be fascinating and helpful 
since I was a
graduate student.  Some years ago I had written up a short exploration of how
useful it could be (at least for me!) to represent CKMR pseudo-likelihoods
via DAGs.  In that case, I was merely trying to understand the calculations
made to account for uncertainty in the paternal or maternal nature of
half-sibling relationships due to limited mtDNA variation in a population.
During the workshop in Hawaii, I found myself wanting to resurrect some of that
early exploration to provide a simple visual language to describe the
CKMR models that we encountered.  Especially since Mark's series of example
CKMR scenarios (Acme Archipelago, Sanctuary Sound, etc.) build upon one another
in complexity, I thought it might be particularly useful to be able to
depict each of those elaborations in DAG form.  This document contains
my attempt to do so.

I have found the process of thinking through a good DAG representation
for the various examples we treated during the course to
reinforce the material we covered last week, and it also provides a visual
way to suggest future extensions.  I know everyone brings their own mental
tools to the understanding of mathematical material.  For some, the following
diagrams might not provide additional insight---or they may even serve to
further confuse the reader!  In such cases I offer my sincere apologies.
I hope, however, that for some of you, the following will provide
a helpful way of visualizing and summarizing the models we encountered.


# The Acme Archipelago

This scenario was the first and simplest one we encountered---estimating
an initial number of females, $N_{0,f}$ and a population growth rate
$\lambda$ using parent offspring pairs from samples with perfectly known ages.  

We consider two distinct, sampled females: a _candidate offspring_, denoted
by the subscript $\mathrm{Ju}$, and a _candidate mother_, denoted by subscript
$\mathrm{Ad}$. These are roles in a comparison: the candidate offspring may
be an adult when sampled, but is called the "juvenile" when being compared as
a candidate offspring.  The females are assumed to become mature when they
reach the age $A_\mathrm{mat}$. 

## A bare-bones DAG

We start with a very simple DAG to express the conditional probability
that an Ad-Ju pair is a parent-offspring pair (POP) given their ages ($A_\Ad$,$A_\Ju$)
and their sampling years ($S_\Ad$, $S_\Ju$).  Included in the DAG is a reference
year $y_0$ that the initial population size corresponds to.

![A bare-bones Acme DAG. Ages, sampling years, and the observed kinship $K$ are gray; parameters are unshaded. Shaded diamonds denote fixed inputs.](figures/acme-bare-bones.pdf){#fig-acme-bare-bones width=80% fig-pos='H'}



The graph represents the marginal probability
of one pair of individuals, _conditioned on their ages and sampling years_
which are taken to be observed without uncertainty, and hence are
shaded gray. $K$ is the kinship of the pair: $K=1$ denotes that they
are a parent offspring pair and $K=0$ denotes they are not.  This is
also shaded because we assume that the pair's relationship is
known without error from genetic data.  This is a proper DAG and it
expresses that the probability that the pair is a POP can be written
as the conditional probability
$$
P(K \mid N_{0,f}, \lambda, y_0, A_\mathrm{mat}, A_\Ju, Y_\Ju, A_\Ad, Y_\Ad).
$$

Wow! That seems singularly unhelpful!  The probability of $K$ depends
on every covariate and parameter in the model.  Tell me something I
don't already know!  

In the next section we will elaborate on this initial bare-bones DAG with some
intermediate variables that I hope will make some of the dependence between
the variables less opaque.  In the meantime, do note that
the CKMR pseudo-likelihood
is formed by multiplying these conditional probabilities over all pairs of individuals.
It is a pseudolikelihood because those pairs are not necessarily independent, though
in large populations under sparse sampling, this can be a good approximation.  As
discussed in the workshop, the product
over all pairs can be reduced to a product of Poisson probabilities over the
different combinations of the juvenile and adult covariates upon which the probabilities
are conditioned (in this case, age and sampling year). 

## A more elaborate DAG

The bare-bones DAG was not particularly helpful: it does very little to elucidate the
dependence structure between the different variables involved.  In many types of models,
introducing some latent variables can provide a refined picture of the
dependence structure (for example, a latent indicator variable in a mixture model).
The calculation of CKMR probabilities is similar. By introducing intermediate
variables or quantities to the DAG, the picture of the dependence structure becomes
more refined.  In the following DAG, we add additional nodes that refine the
dependence structure of the model.  Interestingly, some of these nodes are better
considered "intermediate quantities" rather than "latent variables" because there
is no randomness involved: they are deterministic quantities determined
by their parents in the DAG. We can think of them as degenerate random variables,
and when we insert them into the DAG we mark their nodes with dashed lines.
We also introduce some colors to the DAG to be more explicit about parameters,
covariates, and "observed data," and we introduce a simple error model for
the kinship assignment.

![A single-pair model for the Acme Archipelago represented as an acyclic directed graph (DAG) with several added intermediate nodes.  See the text for explanation.](figures/acme-dag.pdf){#fig-acme width=70% fig-pos='H'}

In the DAG above, light blue fill and double outlines identify the pair-member
covariates upon which we condition. The gray fill of the $K^*$ node denotes an observation;
$K^*$ is the _observed_ relationship of the pair, which might differ from the true
relationship.  Dark pink fill denotes a parameter to be estimated. Nodes with pink outlines mark
quantities whose values (or the conditional distributions of those values) depend
on the parameter values. These are values that must be recalculated
during separate computations of the pseudo-log-likelihood during optimization.
As noted above, dashed nodes identify the added _intermediate quantities_. These values
can be calculated deterministically from their parents and, hence,
could be removed from the model specification; however including them
lets us factorize the DAG more helpfully.  Light blue diamonds denote
fixed inputs or modeling choices.


### Explicit definition of the variables at each node

We use $A$ for age at sampling and $Y$ for year of sampling.
The recorded ages and sampling years are the covariates observed on the samples:
$A_{\mathrm{Ju}}$, $Y_{\mathrm{Ju}}$, $A_{\mathrm{Ad}}$, $Y_{\mathrm{Ad}}$.
In the Acme Archipelago example, we condition on these data, on both individuals
being female, and on the comparison being included in the analysis. Since we are
conditioning on the ages and sampling years (and because they are observed without
error) we do not need to know or specify a distribution for
sampled ages and years to write down this conditional likelihood.

The rose-filled nodes show the parameters. They are $\theta=(N_{0,f},\lambda)$:
adult female abundance at the reference year and an instantaneous exponential
rate of increase, such that $N_{t,f} = N_{0,f}\exp\{\lambda (t - y_0)\}$.
The reference year $y_0$ is a modeling choice, so it is shown as a diamond node.
It is typically set to the earliest juvenile birth year.  It is worth pointing
out here that $N_{0,f}$ counts the number of _mature_ adult females.

There are several intermediate-quantity nodes in the graph.  The first is $B_\Ju$,
the birth year of the juvenile.  This can be calculated simply as $B_\Ju = Y_\Ju - A_\Ju$
The second is $\mathring{A}_\Ad$, the age of the adult at the time of the juveniles
birth. This is calculated from its parents in the DAG by
$\mathring{A}_\Ad = A_\Ad - (Y_\Ad - B_\Ju)$.  The little circle floating above the $A$
in $\mathring{A}_\Ad$ is a notation that we use to mean 
"_at the time of the candidate offspring's birth._"


That little circle appears in $\mathring{R}_\Ad$ to denote
the candidate mother's reproductive 
output at the time of the candidate offspring's birth.  This $\mathring{R}_\Ad$ can
be interpreted as the expected reproductive output of the female adult, and it can
be on a relative scale.  Additional explanation is warranted here for which we go back to
Mark's fundamental equation for the probability of being a POP:
$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{P}[\mbox{Ad~is~Ju's~mum} &\mid \mbox{stuff~about~Ad~and~Ju}] =  \\
\mathbb{E}\biggl[ &\frac
{\#~\mbox{of~Ad's Ju-like offspring at~}B_\Ju}
{\mbox{Total~\#~of~Ju-like~offspring~at~}B_\Ju}
~\biggl | ~
\mbox{stuff (i.e., covariates) about Ad and Ju}
\biggr ]. 
\end{aligned}
$$
In words, this is saying that the probability Ad is Ju's mum, given what we know about
Ad and Ju, is calculated as the expected fraction of all the offspring that "are like"
Ju (i.e., that have the same covariates as Ju) at the time of Ju's birth (i.e., at $B_\Ju$)
that were produced by Ad, given what we know about Ad and Ju (i.e., given the covariates
we have observed on Ad and Ju). This is nothing more than the mathematical statement of
what we learned when discussing "Space toast."  

One thing that we did not talk about in our week in Hawaii is that the above expression
is the expected value of a ratio of two variables.  If the numerator and the denominator
were independent random variables, than the expectation of that ratio would be the
ratio of the expectations.  However, Ad's Ju-like offspring are part of the total output
of Ju-like offspring at $B_\Ju$.  Thus, the numerator and the denominator are not
actually independent.  Nonetheless, if the total number of adults is large and the
variance in output of any one adult is not large, the expectation of the ratio above
is well approximated by the ratio of the expectations, so, it is standard in CKMR
to evaluate the kinship probability as:
$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{P}[&\mbox{Ad~is~Ju's~mum} \mid \mbox{stuff~about~Ad~and~Ju}] \approx  \\
&\frac
{E[\#~\mbox{of~Ad's Ju-like offspring at~}B_\Ju~|~\mbox{stuff (i.e., covariates) about Ad and Ju}]}
{E[\mbox{Total~\#~of~Ju-like~offspring~at~}B_\Ju~|~\mbox{stuff (i.e., covariates) about Ju and the population}]}
\end{aligned}
$$

In the current case, the covariates are simply age and sampling year, and the
expected reproductive output of a female in the population is the same across
all mature females, which simplifies things considerably.  Nonetheless, now, and as we go forward
into the more complex cases, it is worth noting that $\mathring{R}_\Ad$ in
our DAG is the expected value:
$$
\mathring{R}_\Ad \equiv E[\#~\mbox{of~Ad's Ju-like offspring at~}B_\Ju~|~\mbox{stuff (i.e., covariates) about Ad and Ju}],
$$
where "# of offspring" is interpreted as a relative number.
The dependence in that conditional expectation is captured by the arrows in the DAG.
The parents of $\mathring{R}_\Ad$ in the DAG are $B_\Ju$, $\mathring{A}_\Ad$, $Y_\Ad$,
and $A_\mathrm{mat}$, and those are precisely the variables that occur in the
expression for $\mathring{R}_\Ad$, which describes the fact that Ad has reproductive
output typical of any female adult so long as she was mature at $B_\Ju$ and also that
she was not lethally sampled before $B_\Ju$:
$$
\mathring{R}_\Ad = 1\{\mathring{A}_\Ad \geq A_\mathrm{mat}\} 1\{Y_\Ad \geq B_\Ju\}.
$$
This says that if a female is alive and mature at the time of
the offspring's birth she contributes one unit of expected relative output.
The first indicator requires Ad's maturity at Ju's
birth. The second requires that lethal capture of Ad did not precede Ju's birth.
Sampling in Acme Archipelago is strictly after breeding, so equality, 
$Y_{\mathrm{Ad}}=B_{\mathrm{Ju}}$, is allowed.


By a similar turn we define
$$
\mathring{R}_\Tot \equiv 
E[\mbox{Total~\#~of~Ju-like~offspring~at~}B_\Ju~|~\mbox{stuff (i.e., covariates) about Ju and the population}].
$$
This quantity is in the same relative reproductive output units at $\mathring{R}_\Ad$.
Looking at the DAG we see that $\mathring{R}_\Tot$ depends on $N_{0,f}$, $\lambda$, $y_0$, and
$B_\Ju$, and, indeed, we have:

$$
\mathring{R}_\Tot = N_{0,f}\exp\{\lambda(B_{\mathrm{Ju}}-y_0)\}.
$$

$K$ is the true relationship between Ad and Ju.  $K=1$ means Ad is Ju's mother.
$K=0$ means Ad is not Ju's mother, and we have simply:
$$
P(K = 1) = 
\frac{\mathring{R}_\Ad}{\mathring{R}_\Tot}.
$$

$K^*$ is the recorded/detected mother-offspring classification.  We denote the
false positive rate by $\alpha$ and the false negative rate by $\beta$.
These are fixed inputs, not parameters estimated by the likelihood. We generally aim to make 
$\alpha$ negligible and take it as zero, and
the Acme Archipelago example assumes $\alpha=0$ and $\beta=0$. However, it will
be useful, later, to think in terms of genetically _detected_ kin pairs rather than
actual kin pairs, so keeping $K$ latent
and $K^*$ observed, here, makes the detection step explicit even in that special case.
A simple observation error model is:
$$
\begin{aligned}
P(K^* = 1 | K = 1) &= 1-\beta  \\
P(K^* = 0 | K = 1) &= \beta \\
P(K^* = 1 | K = 0) &= \alpha \\
P(K^* = 0 | K = 0) &= 1 - \alpha \\
\end{aligned}
$$
which can be compactly written as:
$$
K^*\mid K,\alpha,\beta
  \sim \operatorname{Bernoulli}(\alpha+(1-\alpha-\beta)K)
$$

### Conditional probabilities implied by the graph

The probability implied by the graph is a product of the conditional
probabities of each node conditional on its (graph) parents.  Since many of
the internal nodes are deterministic, we just include the equation there. 
The hierarchy implied by the DAG is:
$$
\begin{aligned}
B_{\mathrm{Ju}}\mid A_{\mathrm{Ju}},Y_{\mathrm{Ju}}
  &= Y_\mathrm{Ju}-A_\mathrm{Ju},\\[3pt]
\mathring A_{\mathrm{Ad}}\mid A_{\mathrm{Ad}},Y_{\mathrm{Ad}},B_{\mathrm{Ju}}
  &= A_\mathrm{Ad}-(Y_\mathrm{Ad} - B_\mathrm{Ju}),\\[3pt]
\mathring R_{\mathrm{Ad}}\mid\mathring A_{\mathrm{Ad}},Y_{\mathrm{Ad}},B_{\mathrm{Ju}},A_{\mathrm{mat}}
  &= 1\{\mathring{A}_\Ad \geq A_\mathrm{mat}\} 1\{Y_\Ad \geq B_\Ju\},\\[3pt]
\mathring R_{\mathrm{Tot}}\mid N_{0,f},\lambda,B_{\mathrm{Ju}},y_0
  &=N_{0,f}\exp\{\lambda(B_{\mathrm{Ju}}-y_0)\},\\[3pt]
K\mid\mathring R_{\mathrm{Ad}},\mathring R_{\mathrm{Tot}}
  &\sim \operatorname{Bernoulli}\!\left(
       \frac{\mathring R_{\mathrm{Ad}}}{\mathring R_{\mathrm{Tot}}}\right),\\[3pt]
K^*\mid K,\alpha,\beta
  &\sim \operatorname{Bernoulli}\{\alpha+(1-\alpha-\beta)K\}.
\end{aligned}
$$
And we can check that the probability of a true POP occurring (i.e., the
probability of detecting a POP when $\alpha = \beta = 0$) is the familiar
expression:
$$
P(K \mid N_{0,f}, \lambda, y_0, A_\mathrm{mat}, A_\Ju, Y_\Ju, A_\Ad, Y_\Ad) = 
\frac{1\{\mathring{A}_\Ad \geq A_\mathrm{mat}\} 1\{Y_\Ad \geq B_\Ju\}}
{N_{0,f}\exp\{\lambda(B_{\mathrm{Ju}}-y_0)\}}.
$$
